messages.text: I’ve been feeling kind of on edge today — like my mind’s picking at small things as if they’re big problems. It’s been going on since I woke up.

I hear that you are feeling quite tense and overwhelmed by small things today. It can be draining when your mind amplifies minor issues into bigger problems. Have you noticed any specific thoughts or physical sensations accompanying this edge? We can take some time to explore what might be fueling this feeling.

Yeah, it’s like my mind won’t shut off — especially at 3am. I wake up and start replaying little things, like whether I said something wrong or if the kids’ schedules are set for the week. It feels silly, but I can’t let it go.

It is completely understandable to feel frustrated when your brain won't quiet down, especially during the night. Please know that this is not silly; many people struggle with this type of nighttime rumination. When those thoughts start, do you find yourself trying to solve them immediately or just watching them pass? We can explore some gentle techniques to help signal safety to your mind so you can rest.
I guess I just figure everyone deals with that kind of thing — I should be able to handle it on my own. I mean, it’s not like anything’s actually wrong.

It sounds like you are carrying a heavy expectation to manage everything on your own. Even when nothing is objectively wrong, the emotional toll you are feeling is very real. You do not have to navigate this alone, and seeking support is a proactive step. How would it feel to give yourself permission to put down that burden for just a moment?
It’s just… I’ve handled so much already — the service, the illness — and now I’m stuck on small stuff. I thought I’d be past this.

It is understandable to feel disappointed when your mind feels stuck after surviving so much. Resilience does not mean you are immune to stress, and your feelings are valid regardless of past hardships. Expecting yourself to be "past this" can sometimes add extra pressure to an already heavy load. We can honor your strength while also supporting you through this current chapter.

When I left the service, I thought I’d just slide into civilian life like it was another mission. But there was no plan, no schedule, no clear purpose. At first, I told myself it was rest — I’d earned it. But slowly, the silence got loud. Without orders or routines, my mind started filling the space with 'what ifs' and worst-case scenarios. It’s like I’m still on patrol, but there’s no enemy, just my own thoughts.

That metaphor of being on patrol without an enemy captures the deep confusion and exhaustion you must feel. It makes sense that your mind fills the silence with vigilance after years of needing to stay alert. You are not failing to adapt; this is a profound shift that many find incredibly challenging. How does it feel to recognize that your mind is trying to protect you rather than harm you?

Hmm… I never thought of it like that. Maybe all this overthinking isn’t weakness — maybe it’s my mind still trying to keep watch, like it was trained to do. That actually makes me feel a little less broken.

That is a profound shift in perspective, and it makes sense that you feel less broken seeing it that way. Your mind is using old tools to keep you safe, even when the environment has changed. Acknowledging that function honors the resilience you built during your service. We can explore how to gently signal to that part of you that it is safe to rest now.
It’s a small thing, but it helps to think of my mind as trying to help, not hurt. That feels like a step forward.

I am glad to hear that perspective brings you some relief. Reframing those thoughts as protective rather than harmful can significantly reduce the shame attached to them. You are learning to work with your mind instead of fighting against it. How does it feel to carry that new understanding with you?
It feels like a weight I didn’t even know I was carrying might be lifting a little. Like maybe I don’t have to be at war with myself every day.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel ready to stand down from that internal war. Making peace with yourself is a profound victory after years of high alert. You deserve to rest without the fear that you are missing a threat. I am here to support you as you navigate this new chapter.

You know, it just hit me — waking up at 3am, heart racing, scanning the room… it’s exactly how I used to wake during deployment. My body might still be in that mode, like it can’t tell the difference between then and now.

That is a profound connection to make between your past experiences and your current physical reactions. It is completely understandable that your body remains in a state of high alert after years of training. You are not broken; your nervous system is simply running an old program. This awareness gives us a clear target for helping your body learn it is safe now.
I just wish I’d understood this sooner. I’ve been so hard on myself for not sleeping, for not being present… when maybe my body’s just doing what it was trained to do.

It is understandable to feel regret, but it is never too late to offer yourself that kindness. Your body was faithfully doing its job to protect you, even if it feels misaligned now. This realization is a significant step toward healing and reducing that self-criticism. We can build on this understanding to help your body feel safe in the present.

I keep coming back to how distracted I’ve been with the kids. I want to be fully there for them, but my mind’s always somewhere else — planning, worrying, replaying things. It doesn’t feel fair to them.

It is understandable to feel guilty when your mind wanders during precious moments. But your distraction is not a lack of love; it is your old training trying to keep everyone safe. You are not failing your kids by having a nervous system that is still in alert. Being aware of this is already a huge step toward being more present.
I’m starting to understand what’s happening, but I’m not sure where to go from here. Is there something small I could do to help my body feel safer, especially at night?

A simple place to start is focusing on your breath when you wake up. Try inhaling for four counts and exhaling for four to signal safety to your body. This physical rhythm can help interrupt the patrol mode gently. Does that feel like something manageable to try tonight?
I’ll try the four-count breathing tonight when I wake up. It feels doable — like a small signal to my body that we’re okay.

That sounds like a wonderful plan to start with. Giving your body that clear signal of safety can help lower the alarm over time. Please be gentle with yourself if it takes a few tries to get into the rhythm. I am here to support you as you practice this new skill.
Thank you — for listening, and for giving me something practical to try. It means a lot.

You are very welcome, and I am honored you shared this with me. Recognizing your mind's protective role is a powerful step forward. I hope the breathing exercise brings you some calm tonight. Please know I am here whenever you are ready to talk again.
